top_choice_rationale: P003 (Autor, Dorn, Hanson) recognises one achievement when the citation is limited to empirical evidence on labour-demand shocks and local adjustment. Technology and import competition reach workers and places through slow, costly reallocation, and this is measured with shared designs and data. The attribution is traceable to three co-originators, and the core findings have survived a decade or more of replication and criticism of shift-share inference. They matter across labour, trade, macro and public policy. The costs are real. Katz's wage-structure work is excluded, some thematic overlap with the 2021, 2023 and 2024 prizes remains, and the size and persistence of the effects are still debated. I rank the Kiyotaki-Moore pair (P001) second because it has the cleanest attribution and a foundational mechanism that organised a large research programme and passed the 2008 test. Its adjacency to the 2022 prize and the mixed identification of the specific collateral channel keep it just behind. P002 (Berry, Levinsohn, Pakes) is a mature, well-bounded method with a long applied record, so I place it above no award. It ranks third because the omission of Bresnahan, Reiss, Benkard and Levin is a real attribution cost, and because its counterfactuals depend on functional-form and equilibrium assumptions. No award ranks last because several proposals clear the bar on maturity and attribution. This judgement rests on background knowledge, not on independently verified citation data, and not on the number of supporters.
recusal_note: Profile-based connections, disclosed and not adjudicated: I am a frequent co-author of Per Krusell (secretary) and have co-authored with John Hassler (chair). Both are IIES colleagues, and both explicitly support P001 (B006), my second choice. I also have a long-running collaboration with Peter Klenow (B034), which is not on the slate. My heterogeneous-agent macro methods are related to B043, which is also not on the slate. None of Autor, Dorn, Hanson, Kiyotaki, Moore, Berry, Levinsohn or Pakes appears among my listed co-authors, so no direct tie to any proposal's laureates is apparent from the profile.
